newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU health chief attacks tobacco subsidies.
newsitem.headline: EU health chief attacks tobacco subsidies.

text.p: The European Commission's top health official plans to attack European Union tobacco subsidies on Wednesday, arguing they compromise its anti-smoking drive and give its critics ammunition.

Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn, as part of a long battle to cut tobacco-related deaths in the 15-nation bloc, will urge his colleagues to phase out production subsidies in an effort to forge a coherent policy, EU officials said.

"Of perhaps greatest concern is the fact that the existing policy on tobacco is used to attack and discredit Commission policy more generally," he argues in a paper that has been circulated to his colleagues.

However, Flynn is opposed by Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler, who argues that EU member states would never agree to such a radical proposal and that ending subsidies would not curb smoking since the vast majority of tobacco used in the EU is imported.
"If we make a very radical proposal, we end up with the status quo because it won't go anywhere," a Commission agriculture source said, noting that eight EU countries produce tobacco.
Flynn's paper, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, will be discussed during a debate by the 20-member Commission on Wednesday over the future of EU subsidies to tobacco farmers.

The debate is planned to guide the Commission as it draws up two policy papers, one on tobacco farming to be drafted by Fischler and one on initiatives to cut tobacco consumption to be drafted by Flynn.
Flynn complained the EU paid almost 993 million Ecus ($1.25 billion) to support tobacco production in 1995, while devoting only 15 million Ecus a year to discourage smoking.

The EU produces only 5.4 percent of the world's tobacco, but Commission agriculture sources said cutting off tobacco subsidies would put 135,000 farmers and many seasonal workers out of work. EU farmers grow tobacco on small plots averaging one hectare that cannot be easily devoted to other crops, they said.
Italy is the EU's biggest tobacco producer, followed by Greece. Farms are also found in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Portugal and Spain.
Fischler proposes "deepening" reforms that were introduced in 1992, which ended export refunds and public purchases of tobacco and introduced quotas and quality controls.

A Commission agriculture source said Flynn's spending comparisons were unfair because they do not take into account national spending on public health programmes. The EU has sole jurisdiction over tobacco subsidies.
Flynn's paper concedes the EU would have to provide "large-scale" financial assistance to help the tobacco sector adjust if it abolished subsidies.
But he complained the quality of EU tobacco is on average so low that its commercial value is only one fifth of the subsidies that are used to grow it.
